title: Germany Is Out. Paraguay's Goalkeeper Rewrote World Cup History in Boston.
excerpt: Orlando Gill saved two penalties as Paraguay stunned the four-time champions 4-3 in a shootout — Germany's first-ever World Cup penalty loss. The tournament's biggest upset yet unfolded 30 miles from downtown Boston, in front of thousands of diaspora fans.
body:
Germany came to Foxborough as four-time World Cup winners, unbeaten in five penalty shootouts across 44 years of tournament football. They left as the first major casualty of the 2026 knockout stage, eliminated by a team ranked 31 places below them — in the least German way imaginable.

Paraguay beat Germany 4-3 on penalty kicks on Monday night at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, after the two sides drew 1-1 through 120 minutes of regulation and extra time. It was the biggest upset of the 2026 World Cup so far, and it ended one of the sport's most ironclad records.

## Gill Was Everywhere

The hero was Orlando Gill, Paraguay's 26-year-old goalkeeper, who turned in the performance of his life. He saved Kai Havertz's opening penalty, diving to his left with perfect timing. When Nick Woltemade stepped up for Germany's fourth attempt, Gill stopped that too, diving low to deny what should have been the go-ahead kick.

Between those two saves, Gill had already kept Paraguay alive in regulation and extra time with a string of crucial stops. In the 76th minute, he denied Havertz from point-blank range after a Florian Wirtz cross. In the 105th minute, he swallowed a dangerous header by Waldemar Anton off a corner kick. In the 118th minute, he collected another German header that seemed destined for the back of the net.

"I think the feeling we have is difficult to explain," Paraguay captain Gustavo Gomez said in a post-match interview. "I think deep down Germany knew that if they wanted to beat us, they would have to sweat blood, because we were going to make defeat very, very expensive for them."

## Enciso Struck First

For all of Germany's possession dominance — they controlled 84 per cent of the ball in the first half — it was Paraguay that struck first. In the 42nd minute, Matias Galarza delivered a cross from the left, and Julio Enciso, Brighton's 21-year-old forward, met it with a textbook header into the lower corner. Manuel Neuer had no chance.

Germany equalized eight minutes into the second half. Wirtz, arguably the tournament's most dangerous creator, whipped a cross into the box, and Havertz headed it home. The pattern of the match was set: Germany pushed, Paraguay absorbed and counter-punched, and Gill was the wall.

Extra time brought the game's most dramatic sequence. Jonathan Tah rose to head in a corner kick in the 102nd minute, and Gillette Stadium erupted. But a VAR review found a foul in the build-up, and the goal was wiped off the board. It was the kind of ruling that can break a team's spirit — and for Germany, it did.

## The Shootout

When penalties came, Germany's record stood at a perfect 5-0 in World Cup shootouts — victories over France (1982), Mexico (1986), England (1990), and Argentina (2006). No other nation had such a spotless record from the spot.

Gill changed that in under ten minutes.

After his two saves, the shootout lurched into sudden death. Neuer pulled off a save of his own to deny Fabian Balbuena and keep Germany alive. But Tah, who had already endured the agony of a disallowed goal, sent his sudden-death penalty sailing over the crossbar. Jose Canale stepped up and buried the winner.

Paraguayans in the stands were crying. Germans stood motionless, hands on heads.

## Germany's Barren Decade

For Germany, this was more than a bad night. It was the latest chapter in a decade-long decline that has seen one of football's greatest powers become a serial underperformer at major tournaments:

- **World Cup 2018** — group stage exit
- **World Cup 2022** — group stage exit
- **Euro 2024** — quarter-final exit (at home)
- **World Cup 2026** — Round of 32 exit

Julian Nagelsmann, at 38 the youngest coach in a World Cup knockout stage in 40 years, will face enormous pressure when the squad returns home.

"I am disappointed. It was just not enough to beat this opponent," Nagelsmann told reporters after the match. "We lost control of possession. We tried a lot of things but we should have scored earlier."

## What It Means for Indian Fans in North America

The 2026 World Cup has become the first truly immersive sporting spectacle for the Indian diaspora in North America — and Foxborough, just 30 miles from downtown Boston, sits in one of the most densely Indian-American corridors in the northeastern United States.

Monday's drama unfolded in a stadium surrounded by the universities, tech corridors, and suburban communities that have drawn hundreds of thousands of Indian immigrants and their families over the past two decades. The match was the kind of high-stakes, chaotic, penalty-laden theater that converts neutral fans into lifelong followers. For many Indian-Americans, especially those who grew up with cricket but are now embracing football, this World Cup offers a unique opportunity to witness global sporting history firsthand, fostering a deeper connection to their adopted homes and the international community.

The tournament is about to come even closer. On Wednesday, the United States takes on Bosnia and Herzegovina at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California — the heart of Silicon Valley, and home to one of the largest Indian-American populations in the country. That match kicks off at 1 PM Pacific, and tickets in the Bay Area have been selling briskly among diaspora fans eager to experience a World Cup knockout game on their doorstep. Many Indian tech professionals and families are planning watch parties, turning these games into community events that bridge cultural divides and celebrate shared passions.

Paraguay now awaits the winner of Tuesday's France vs Sweden match at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The Round of 16 clash is set for July 4 in Philadelphia — another city with a thriving Indian-American community. The excitement among the diaspora is palpable, with many seeing these matches as a chance to connect with global sports culture while celebrating their presence in North America.

## Monday's Other Result

Earlier in the day, Brazil edged Japan 2-1 in Houston after Gabriel Martinelli scored a dramatic goal six minutes into stoppage time. Brazil advances to the Round of 16, where they will face the winner of Tuesday's Norway vs Ivory Coast match.
